facts.text: The only pitcher of the 1980s to strike out 200 and win 9 games or fewer: Nolan Ryan Jr., 1987 — 270 K, 8-16.
The only pitcher of the 1980s to throw 300 innings: Steve Carlton, 1980 — 304.0 IP.
The only hitter of the 1980s to drive in 100 runs with 8 homers or fewer: Tom Herr, 1985 — 110 RBI, 8 HR.
The only hitter of the 1980s to go 40-40: José Canseco, 1988 — 42 HR, 40 SB.
The only hitter of the 1980s to bat .320 at age 37 or older (500+ PA): Rod Carew, 1983 — .339 at 37.
Only two pitchers of the 1980s struck out 300 without winning 20: Mike Scott (1986, 306 K, 18-10); Nolan Ryan Jr. (1989, 301 K, 16-10).
Only two pitchers of the 1980s walked 130+ batters: Bobby Witt (1986, 143 BB); Bobby Witt (1987, 140 BB).
The only pitcher of the 1980s to save 30 games with an ERA of 4.25 or worse: Jeff Reardon, 1987 — 31 SV, 4.48 ERA.
The only pitcher of the 1980s to win 25 games: Steve Stone, 1980 — 25-7.
The only pitcher of the 1980s to lose 20 games: Brian Kingman, 1980 — 8-20.
The only pitcher of the 1980s to post an ERA under 3.00 and win 7 or fewer (162+ IP): Joe Magrane, 1988 — 2.18 ERA, 5-9.
Only two hitters of the 1980s score 120 runs with 50 RBI or fewer: Willie Wilson (1980, 133 R, 49 RBI); Vince Coleman (1987, 121 R, 43 RBI).
The only pitcher of the 1980s to win 15 games walking 30 batters or fewer: LaMarr Hoyt, 1985 — 16-8, 20 BB.
Only two hitters of the 1980s hit 45 doubles and 5 homers or fewer: Wade Boggs (1989, 51 2B, 3 HR); Wade Boggs (1988, 45 2B, 5 HR).
Just three hitters of the 1980s drew 100 walks and struck out 140 times: Jack Clark (1989, 132 BB, 145 K); Mike Schmidt (1983, 128 BB, 148 K); Jack Clark (1988, 113 BB, 141 K).
Mike Schmidt hit 30+ home runs in 8 straight seasons (1980-87), the longest run of the 1980s.
Rickey Henderson stole 40+ bases in 10 straight seasons (1980-89), the longest run of the 1980s.
Only two hitters of the 1980s went 20-20 while batting under .240: Dwayne Murphy (1982, 27 HR, 26 SB, .238); Howard Johnson (1988, 24 HR, 23 SB, .230).
Only two hitters of the 1980s hit 35+ homers with 15 doubles or fewer: Dave Kingman (1982, 37 HR, 9 2B); Bob Horner (1980, 35 HR, 14 2B).
Only two hitters of the 1980s batted .320 or better with 25 walks or fewer (500+ PA): Mickey Rivers (1980, .333, 20 BB); Kirby Puckett (1988, .356, 23 BB).

Just three hitters of the 1980s batted .300 with 30 homers, 100 RBI and 20 steals: José Canseco (1988, .307, 42 HR, 124 RBI, 40 SB); Dale Murphy (1983, .302, 36 HR, 121 RBI, 30 SB); Pedro Guerrero (1982, .304, 32 HR, 100 RBI, 22 SB).
Only two pitchers of the 1980s posted an ERA under 2.00 (162+ IP): Dwight Gooden (1985, 1.53 ERA in 276.2 IP); John Tudor (1985, 1.93 ERA in 275.0 IP).
Fernando Valenzuela threw 250+ innings in 6 straight seasons (1982-87), the longest run of the 1980s.
Just four pitchers of the 1980s saved 45 games: Dave Righetti (1986, 46 SV); Dan Quisenberry (1983, 45 SV); Bruce Sutter (1984, 45 SV); Dennis Eckersley (1988, 45 SV).
Dave Winfield drove in 100+ runs in 5 straight seasons (1982-86), the longest run of the 1980s.
Jeff Reardon saved 30+ games in 5 straight seasons (1985-89), the longest run of the 1980s.
Just three hitters of the 1980s stole 30+ bases and was caught 3 times or fewer: Jack Perconte (1985, 31 SB, 2 CS); Eric Davis (1988, 35 SB, 3 CS); Tom Herr (1985, 31 SB, 3 CS).

Just four pitchers of the 1980s won 18+ games at age 22 or younger: Dwight Gooden (1985, 24-4 at 20); Bret Saberhagen (1985, 20-6 at 21); Fernando Valenzuela (1982, 19-13 at 21); Greg Maddux (1988, 18-8 at 22).
14 times in the 1980s a hitter played a full season without a single home run (600+ PA). The most extreme: Jerry Remy, 1982 — 0 HR in 716 PA.
25 times in the 1980s a hitter stole 70 bases. The most extreme: Rickey Henderson, 1982 — 130 SB.
Lowest average by any 100-RBI hitter of the 1980s: Tony Armas, 1983 — .218 with 107 RBI.
Most strikeouts by a .300 hitter of the 1980s: Andres Galarraga, 1988 — 153 K while batting .302.
Most steals by a 30-homer hitter of the 1980s: Eric Davis, 1987 — 50 SB with 37 HR.
Most home runs per RBI of the 1980s: Brook Jacoby, 1987 — 32 HR but only 69 RBI.
Fewest strikeouts by a 30-homer hitter of the 1980s: Don Mattingly, 1986 — 35 K with 31 HR.
Highest average by a hitter with 3 homers or fewer: Miguel Dilone, 1980 — .341 with 0 HR.
Most walks by a sub-.240 hitter of the 1980s: Dwayne Murphy, 1982 — 94 BB while batting .238.
Most wins by a pitcher with an ERA over 5.00: Dan Spillner, 1980 — 16-11 with a 5.28 ERA.
Fewest wins by a qualified pitcher with an ERA under 3.00: Joe Magrane, 1988 — 5-9 despite a 2.18 ERA.
Most strikeouts by a pitcher with a losing record: Steve Carlton, 1983 — 275 K, 15-16.
Most losses by a pitcher with an ERA under 3.50: Bruce Berenyi, 1982 — 9-18 with a 3.36 ERA.
Fewest strikeouts by a 20-game winner of the 1980s: Tommy John, 1980 — 78 K, 22-9.
Most home runs allowed in a season this decade: Bert Blyleven, 1986 — 50 HR allowed, 17-14.
Most walks by a 15-game winner: Charlie Hough, 1988 — 126 BB, 15-16.
21 hitter-seasons of the 1980s ended on exactly 29 home runs, one short of 30 — among them Dwight Evans (1985), Joe Carter (1986), Eddie Murray (1984).
11 hitter-seasons of the 1980s ended on exactly 99 RBI, one short of 100 — among them Keith Hernandez (1980), Andre Thornton (1984), Cecil Cooper (1985).
Mark Langston struck out 200+ in 4 straight seasons (1986-89), the longest run of the 1980s.
7 teams of the 1980s won 100 games; the best record was the 1986 Mets at 108-54.
6 hitter-seasons of the 1980s ended on a .299 average, one point short of .300 — among them Bill Buckner (1985), Andre Dawson (1983), Keith Hernandez (1982).
Oldest player of the 1980s to hit 30 home runs: Darrell Evans, age 40 in 1987 — 34 HR.
Youngest player of the 1980s to bat .330 (500+ PA): Don Mattingly, age 23 in 1984 — .343.
Oldest player of the 1980s to bat .330 (500+ PA): Rod Carew, age 37 in 1983 — .339.
Oldest player of the 1980s to drive in 100 runs: Tony Perez, age 38 in 1980 — 105 RBI.
Oldest player of the 1980s to steal 40 bases: Davey Lopes, age 40 in 1985 — 47 SB.
Oldest player of the 1980s to win 20 games: Tommy John, age 37 in 1980 — 22-9.
Oldest player of the 1980s to post a qualified ERA under 2.75: Bert Blyleven, age 38 in 1989 — 2.73 ERA.
3 teams of the 1980s had two players at 35+ home runs; the biggest pairing was the 1980 Milwaukee Brewers — Ben Oglivie 41, Gorman Thomas 38.
3 teams of the 1980s had three players at 100+ RBI; the biggest pairing was the 1982 Milwaukee Brewers — Cecil Cooper 121, Robin Yount 114, Gorman Thomas 112.
18 teams of the 1980s had two players at 40+ steals; the biggest pairing was the 1988 St. Louis Cardinals — Vince Coleman 81, Ozzie Smith 57, Willie McGee 41.
3 teams of the 1980s had two players at 20 wins; the biggest pairing was the 1983 Chicago White Sox — LaMarr Hoyt 24, Richard Dotson 22.
Most home runs in the 1980s by a hitter who never led the majors in a season: Dale Murphy, 308.
Most hits of the 1980s: Robin Yount, 1731.
Most triples of the 1980s: Willie Wilson, 115.
Most RBI of the 1980s: Eddie Murray, 996.
Most wins of the 1980s: Jack Morris, 162.
Most losses of the 1980s: Jim Clancy, 126 — and 119 wins.
Most complete games of the 1980s: Jack Morris, 133.
1987 had 28 30-homer hitters, the most of any season in the 1980s.
1981 had just 1 30-homer hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1980s.
1980 had 33 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the most of any season in the 1980s.
1981 had no .300 hitters (500+ PA) at all — the only season of the 1980s without one.
1987 had 23 100-RBI hitters, the most of any season in the 1980s.
1981 had no 100-RBI hitters at all — the only season of the 1980s without one.
1980 had 17 40-steal players, the most of any season in the 1980s.
1981 had just 3 40-steal players, the fewest of any season in the 1980s.
1986 had 8 200-hit seasons, the most of any season in the 1980s.
1981 had no 200-hit seasons at all — the only season of the 1980s without one.
1980 had 7 20-game winners, the most of any season in the 1980s.
1981 had no 20-game winners at all — the only season of the 1980s without one.
11 teams of the 1980s lost 100 games; the worst was the 1988 Orioles at 54-107.
Best run differential of the 1980s: the 1986 Mets, +205 (783 scored, 578 allowed).
6 times in the 1980s a hitter hit 30+ homers at age 37 or older. The most extreme: Darrell Evans, 1985 — 40 HR at 38.
18 times in the 1980s a pitcher won 15+ games at age 38 or older. The most extreme: Phil Niekro, 1985 — 16-12 at 46.
Exactly one hitter of the 1980s finished a season with exactly 199 hits, one short of 200: Kirby Puckett (1985).
Exactly one hitter of the 1980s finished a season with exactly 49 steals, one short of 50: Steve Sax (1982).
Exactly one pitcher of the 1980s finished a season with exactly 39 saves, one short of 40: John Franco (1988).
Worst run differential of the 1980s: the 1988 Orioles, -239 (550 scored, 789 allowed).
9 times in the 1980s a hitter grounded into 28+ double plays. The most extreme: Jim Rice, 1984 — 36 GIDP.
11 times in the 1980s a hitter got hit by 15+ pitches. The most extreme: Don Baylor, 1986 — 35 HBP.
5 times in the 1980s a hitter stole 40+ bases with an on-base under .300 (400+ PA). The most extreme: Omar Moreno, 1982 — 60 SB, .292 OBP.
13 times in the 1980s a pitcher completed 18+ games. The most extreme: Rick Langford, 1980 — 28 CG.
5 times in the 1980s a hitter drew more walks than hits (400+ PA). The most extreme: Gene Tenace, 1980 — 92 BB, 70 H.
7 times in the 1980s a hitter struck out 25 times or fewer in a full season (600+ PA). The most extreme: Bill Buckner, 1980 — 18 K in 615 PA.
5 times in the 1980s a hitter hit 30+ homers while batting under .230 (400+ PA). The most extreme: Dave Kingman, 1982 — 37 HR, .204.
15 times in the 1980s a pitcher won 12+ games without a start. The most extreme: Mark Clear, 1982 — 14-9, 0 GS.
5 times in the 1980s a hitter hit 30+ homers at age 22 or younger. The most extreme: Bob Horner, 1980 — 35 HR at 22.
6 times in the 1980s a pitcher threw 8+ shutouts. The most extreme: John Tudor, 1985 — 10 SHO.

method: Every fact is a predicate evaluated over every hitter-season and pitcher-season in the decade, pulled in full from the MLB Stats API (the official record). Nothing is recalled or estimated; the rows that satisfy each rule are stored with it.

'Only', 'two' and 'three/four' claims are exact counts across the complete pull. Where a rule uses a plate-appearance or innings floor instead of a league qualification bar, the floor is stated in the fact so the claim is reproducible.
Thresholds are era-aware (strikeouts, saves and home runs meant different things in 1925 and 1995) and are recorded in the file.
Rules built from plain comparisons carry a Stathead Season Finder spec with the same filters and year range, for independent re-checking on the subscription.
